segments.t: Early in the morning at ASK, Andréa arrives looking radiant after an all-night conversation with Fabrice Luchini. She shares the thrilling breakthrough with Arlette and Mathias: Luchini has broken with rival agent François Bréhier. Listen to the scene in French first.
On a passé une folle nuit?
Exactement! Devinez avec qui.
Avec qui?
Fabrice Luchini.
Non. Il ne fallait pas aller jusque-là.
Non... c'était fou et platonique.
Il a quitté Bréhier.
C'est une excellente nouvelle! J'adore!
Calme-toi, Arlette.
Quel rabat-joie!
On a parlé toute la nuit, j'adore ce type.
Je crois qu'il m'aime bien aussi.
Je ne comprends pas. Il a dit oui?
Pas encore, mais il m'a invitée au théâtre ce soir.
On ne fête pas ça trop vite, mais ça s'annonce bien!
Tu vois, Mathias? Il fallait juste oser.
Let's explore Andréa's triumphant morning debrief line by line.
On a passé une folle nuit?
'Did we have a wild night?' Arlette teases Andréa's disheveled and glowing appearance. In French, you'd use a phrasing that translates literally as 'we have passed'. This is very typical in French.
Exactement! Devinez avec qui.
'Exactly! Guess with whom.' Andréa hypes up the mystery. You'll hear this command when someone wants you to solve a puzzle. A common chunk in French.
Avec qui?
'With whom?' Mathias asks with dry skepticism. This handy phrase literally means 'with who'. You will hear this in French.
Fabrice Luchini.

'None other than Fabrice Luchini.' Andréa drops the superstar name triumphantly. Unlike English, the original just states the name without adding 'None other than'. This is perfectly natural in French.
Non. Il ne fallait pas aller jusque-là.
'No. You shouldn't have gone that far.' Mathias immediately suspects a scandal. It is built from the idea of 'it was not necessary to go'. In French, it works nicely.
Non... c'était fou et platonique.
'No... it was wild and platonic.' Andréa sets the record straight. You can use these two near cognates to describe an innocent but crazy evening. The French use this a lot.
Il a quitté Bréhier.
'He left Bréhier.' Andréa delivers the crucial agency intelligence. This translates closer to 'He has left'. In French, it sounds perfect.
C'est une excellente nouvelle! J'adore!
'That is excellent news! I love it!' Arlette rejoices at their rival's loss. You can say this whenever you hear something fantastic. This is standard in French.
Calme-toi, Arlette.
'Calm down, Arlette.' Mathias tries to maintain composure. He uses the casual 'you' command to tell his colleague to relax. A nice sentence in French.
Quel rabat-joie!
'What a killjoy!' Arlette mocks Mathias's perpetual pessimism. Literally 'strikes joy', this idiom is perfect for a party pooper. A great expression in French.
On a parlé toute la nuit, j'adore ce type.
'We talked all night, I adore this guy.' Andréa describes their deep mutual connection. You'd use this to say you really like someone's personality. You can say this in French.
Je crois qu'il m'aime bien aussi.
'I think that he likes me too.' Andréa notes their instant chemistry. In French, you place 'me' before the action 'likes'. In French, this is widely used.
Je ne comprends pas. Il a dit oui?
'I don't understand. Did he say yes?' Mathias demands practical confirmation. This handy sentence translates as 'He has said yes?'. The French love this expression.
Pas encore, mais il m'a invitée au théâtre ce soir.
'Not yet, but he invited me to the theatre tonight.' Andréa reveals her follow-up date. This means 'he has invited me'. In French, it fits perfectly.
On ne fête pas ça trop vite, mais ça s'annonce bien!
'Let's not celebrate too quickly, but it looks promising!' Andréa cautions prudence while staying optimistic. It translates closer to 'it announces itself well'. A nice way to say it in French.
Tu vois, Mathias? Il fallait juste oser.

'You see, Mathias? We just had to dare.' Andréa proudly claims credit for taking the risk. Literally 'it was necessary just to dare', this is a very natural way to express taking a chance. In French, it is a great choice. Now let's listen to the whole debriefing once more from start to finish.
On a passé une folle nuit?
Exactement! Devinez avec qui.
Avec qui?
Fabrice Luchini.
Non. Il ne fallait pas aller jusque-là.
Non... c'était fou et platonique.
Il a quitté Bréhier.
C'est une excellente nouvelle! J'adore!
Calme-toi, Arlette.
Quel rabat-joie!
On a parlé toute la nuit, j'adore ce type.
Je crois qu'il m'aime bien aussi.
Je ne comprends pas. Il a dit oui?
Pas encore, mais il m'a invitée au théâtre ce soir.
On ne fête pas ça trop vite, mais ça s'annonce bien!
Tu vois, Mathias? Il fallait juste oser.
Andréa has pulled off a diplomatic masterstroke, opening the door for Luchini to join ASK. Remember the key verb for taking a bold chance: oser. See you next time!
Bonne journée!
